title: Flour or flower? A tiny word puzzle for your ears
description: Meet homophones: words that sound alike but mean different things. Try three paired clues, then test another kind of connection.

cover.alt: A bowl of flour beside a yellow flower in a small glass vase
cover.credit: AI-generated photorealistic illustration created for BrainiLab.

sections.title: A shopping list with a possible misunderstanding
sections.html:
Someone asks you to bring a flower. You arrive with a bag of flour. The cake might be rescued; the bouquet is another matter.

Homophones are words pronounced alike that have different meanings. Their spellings can differ too. Merriam-Webster gives to, too and two as an example. Its entries for flour and flower also show the same pronunciation.

The useful clue is often outside the word. A vase suggests one meaning; a recipe suggests the other. Try saying a pair aloud, then put each word into a sentence.

sections.title: Three pairs to untangle
sections.html:
Find two different words for each pair of clues. The answers should sound the same. Read them aloud before opening the answer.

  1. A baking ingredient / something with petals.
  2. A chess piece that can jump / the time after sunset.
  3. A number after one / also.
Check the pairs

Flour / flower. Knight / night. Two / too. In the third pair, “I want two biscuits” counts them; “I want a biscuit too” adds another person to the request.

Now write one deliberately silly sentence using both words from a pair. A knight who only rides at night? That works. The aim is to make the meanings distinct even when the sounds are identical.

sections.title: Same sound is only one possible link
sections.html:
Look at flour, sugar, butter, eggs. Their shared link is meaning: they can be baking ingredients. Compare flour and flower. That link is sound. “Connected” does not always mean “in the same category”.

This matters in a word puzzle: test the proposed relationship against every clue. If a sound-based idea fits only half the words, keep looking. Our Connections guide shows how to check a candidate link without making exceptions.

sections.title: Your pronunciation matters
sections.html:
A sound-based puzzle depends on how words are pronounced. If a pair does not sound alike in your accent, check the pronunciation guide before deciding you missed something.

For a different twist, meet words that can mean their own opposite. There the surprise comes from meaning, even when the spelling stays exactly the same.

practice: Try Connections and look for a relationship that fits every clue. It might involve meaning, a category or another shared feature.
